  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  August 25, 2025
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:06 p.m., on Monday, August 25, 2025, the Alhambra City Council met in the Council
Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager
Hembree, City Attorney Montes, City Clerk Myles, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director
of Finance Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Principal Planner McCurley, Director of
Public Works and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Police Kennedy, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Director
of Library Services LohGuan, Director of Human Resources Ko, Management Analyst Alvarez, Public
Information Specialist Rodriguez

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Lee

ANDRADE-STADLER:  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER requested that Item No. 2 be
moved to after Public Comment for Non-Agendized Items due to the number of speakers as well as
the number of student speakers in the audience. Mayor LEE agreed to the change in agenda order.

LEE: Mayor Lee read the City’s Mission Statement as follows: The City of Alhambra is dedicated to
responsive, creative leadership and quality services, ensuring desirable neighborhoods and a
supportive business environment, while being sensitive to the diversity of our community.

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

PRESENTATIONS

2.  CONSIDERATION OF SUPPORTING THE ALHAMBRA  TEACHERS  ASSOCIATION
  FOOD PANTRY – F2M25-7, F2M25-17, M2M25-123
  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER provided information regarding the item. At the July
  28, 2025 Council Meeting, Councilmember Andrade-Stadler requested a donation of
  $60,000.00 to the Alhambra teachers Association (ATA) Food Pantry. A request from ATA
  and Urban Visionaries was subsequently submitted to the City for the amount of $60,000.00.
  Urban Visionaries and ATA sought to address food insecurity, provide immigrant resources
  and address systematic barriers faced by Alhambra students and families. The funding would
  assist approximately 500 Alhambra students and families. A donation of $60,000.00 would
  require a draw down from the General Fund Reserves. The Alhambra Municipal Code and
  Resolution No. R2M25-8 establish the placement of the General Fund Reserves, which are
  one-time unappropriated surplus funds for the City’s unanticipated or deferred needs. A target
  of 30% in General Fund Reserves has been established by the City Council and was included
  in the City’s 2025 Strategic Plan. The current reserve balance is 20.6%, or $20,578,968. If
  approved, an account number and transfer of $60,00.00 from the general fund will be initiated.
  Li’i Furimoto, representing Urban Visionaries, and Tammi Scorcia, representing the Alhambra
  Teachers Association, were present to answer questions.

  Public Comment:

  The following people spoke in favor of the item:
  1) Tammy Scorcia, 1318 E. Dalton Ave., Glendora, representing the Alhambra Teachers
  Association
  2) Li’i Furumoto, 3030 W. Main St., representing Urban Visionaries
  3) Demitri Vera, resident at Atlantic and Main
  4) Jay Xu, 22 South El Molino St.
  5) Barry Tang, 1809 Pepper Street
  6) Shirley Tatsuno, 1408 S. Fifth St.
  7) Lucas Yu, a resident of 4th St.
  8) Edward Escarsega, via Zoom, also made suggestions for accountability and for the city to draw
  up a Memorandum of Understanding.

  The following person spoke against the item:
  1) Ron Sahu, via Zoom, also submitted his comments via email which are on file in the City Clerk’s
  office.

  2
8-25-25
   The following people made additional comments:
  1) Jennifer NG, S. Cordova St., asked for clarification regarding community outreach and asked
  for clarification regarding community donations. She supported the organization but questioned
  the precedent set by the City making a donation with public funds. She questioned why the
  organization had not sought out 501(c)(3) status.

  2) Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., reported that he had received an email from Mr. Sahu
  regarding his concerns and went on to discuss additional information. He spoke in support of
  the organization and made suggestions for policies for future donations going forward as well
  as accountability reports from organizations. He also supported Ms. Ng’s comments regarding
  the organization’s status as a tax-exempt charity organization.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA spoke in support of the Alhambra Teachers Association
  (ATA) and the Food Pantry. He discussed the Council’s role as responsible stewards of the
  City’s money. Mr. MAZA and Ms. FURUMOTO discussed Urban Visionaries and their
  relationship with Alhambra Unified School District (AUSD) in assessing the families in need,
  as well as their partnership with other organizations and agencies to procure the food for the
  Pantry. Mr. MAZA and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the Reserve Funds. Mr. MAZA and Ms.
  FURUMOTO went on to discuss how Urban Visionaries has worked to make the Food Pantry
  sustainable to meet the needs of the community through partnership with other agencies to
  procure food as well as their occasional purchase of culturally specific food items for families.
  Mr. MAZA stated that he supported the donation although he stated that Council needed to be
  careful moving forward with the City reserve funds. He added that Council could make
  personal donations from their City stipends and committed to his own such donation.

  Vice Mayor MALONEY spoke regarding food and housing insecurity in the community and
  stated that in a larger sense, this qualified as an emergency with regards to additional concerns
  in the community related to federal immigration enforcement. He stated that the Council did
  have some latitude and discretion with the reserve fund and that he would support this
  donation. Mr. MALONEY and Ms. FURUMOTO discussed why the money would be allocated
  to Urban Visionaries as a 501(c)(3) organization working with ATA. Ms. FURUMOTO
  explained the relationship between Urban Visionaries, ATA, and AUSD as well as the roles
  taken by each group. Ms. FURUMOTO and Mr. MALONEY discussed how the money would
  be used from this one-time donation, as well as Urban Visionaries plans to secure future
  funding sources. Mr. MALONEY went on to discuss the need for the Food Pantry to have a
  more sustainable plan for the future, the difficulties in relying on donations, and the
  appropriateness of using general fund reserve money. He suggested that Urban Visionaries
  consider devoting 10% of funds to dedicated administrative costs in order to create a plan to
  seek grants for program deliverables. He suggested that the City create an actual agreement
  of Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Urban Visionaries that would outline all
  parameters and what the deliverables would be. He further requested this include copies of
  receipts and timesheets for public transparency. He cited similar agreements with other groups
  and requested a report in 6 months to Council. He emphasized the importance of an
  agreement that would describe the scope of work and create transparency for the public in
  identifying deliverables. He echoed Mr. Maza in stressing that this was a one-time grant and
  that Council would have to be more careful about spending reserve funds in the future.

  Councilmember WANG spoke regarding the need in the community but added that she wanted
  to understand the agreement. Ms. WANG, City Manager BINNQUIST, and Ms. FURUMOTO
  further discussed the relationship between Urban Visionaries, ATA, and AUSD in the operation
  of the Food Pantry. Ms. WANG and Ms. BINNQUIST went on to discuss the City’s lack of a
  framework for evaluating support for non-profits, the lack of previous precedent of donations,
  service agreement contracts with other non-profit organizations, the Reserve Fund Policy, and
  Strategic Plan Goals related to the Reserve Funds. Ms. WANG expressed concerns with the
  donation and the appropriateness of using reserve funds for a one-time donation. She went
  3
8-25-25
   on to discuss the purpose of the Reserve Fund, the need to maintain a reserve fund in case
  of an economic downturn, the need for a policy or procedure to spend taxpayer funds in an
  equitable and fair manner. She added that she would also be happy to personally donate as
  suggested by Mr. Maza or to assist in any way with fundraising or volunteering. She referred
  to the proposal submitted where a majority of funds would go to a multilingual coordinator and
  suggested that rather than a donation, that Council delegate City Board and Commission
  members help to find volunteers to help in this effort. She further suggested that the City help
  identify grants for Urban Visionaries. She stated that should Council identify food insecurity as
  a priority, then they should create a policy to handle similar requests. She stated that she would
  like a process similar to other City contract agreements associated with an approved Request
  for Proposal process.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the Reserve Fund.
  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER made a motion to approve the donation with additions suggested
  by Mr. Maloney to include a report back to Council in 6 months, to increase the administrative
  allotment to 6%, and to draft an MOU with the City. She stated that she understood her
  colleagues’ concerns, but added that these were unprecedented times with families in need.
  She agreed that there needed to be a stronger process in place for donations.

  Mayor LEE discussed her past relationship with ATA and expressed concern with donating to
  an organization with which she was personally associated with. She went on to discuss the
  Reserve Fund and the need for a process to make donations from the fund. Ms. LEE and City
  Attorney MONTES discussed state laws regarding the use of public funds as a gift for both
  charter law cities and general law cities. Ms. LEE went on to discuss the Reserve Fund Policy
  in place and stated that she did not support the donation without an agendized discussion to
  amend the policy. She went on to question naming ATA in the agreement when the money
  would go to Urban Visionaries. She further discussed the need to maintain the Reserve Fund
  for use in cases of emergency or economic downturn. Ms. LEE made a substitute motion to
  table the item until Council could have an agendized discussion to amend the Reserve Fund
  Policy to include donations or gifts.

  Mr. MALONEY seconded Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s motion, but offered amendments to her
  motion. He suggested that the language be amended to omit mention of ATA since it would be
  going to Urban Visionaries, requested that this be called a grant rather than a donation, and
  requested a grant agreement which would allow for legal requirements of the grantee. He
  further suggested a moratorium for any future expenditures of the General Fund Reserves for
  similar requests from non-profits for grants, until staff and Council could develop a policy under
  the Reserve Fund Policy as well as a separate policy for grant agreements. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER accepted the amendments to her motion and called for the vote.

  Ms. LEE repeated her substitute motion on the table. Mr. MALONEY and Ms. LEE discussed
  his amendments. Ms. LEE asked if Staff would draft the grant agreement, which Mr.
  MALONEY confirmed. Ms. LEE asked if Mr. Maloney would consider an additional amendment
  to reduce the cost. Mr. MALONEY offered an explanation regarding operating costs of
  nonprofits but declined the suggestion. They continued to discuss the role of volunteers versus
  paid coordinators as well as donating money for food procurement as opposed to
  administrative costs. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER called again for the vote on her motion.

  Ms. LEE stated that she would not support the donation. Ms. WANG expressed concern with
  the donation and seconded Ms. Lee’s substitute motion to table discussion until Council and
  staff could develop a criteria. Ms. LEE restated her motion to table the discussion, which Ms.
  WANG seconded. Ms. LEE called for the vote on her motion. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. MONTES
  discussed Rosenberg’s Rules of Order in which case the substitute motion would be voted on
  before the original motion.

  4
8-25-25
   SUBSTITUTE MOTION: To table the item until Council and staff could draft a donation
  program which would reflect equity, fairness, and accountability for the future.

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  WANG, LEE
  Noes:  MALONEY, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER
  Absent:  NONE

  The motion failed.

  Council next voted on the amended original motion to draft a grant agreement between the
  City of Alhambra and Urban Visionaries for $60,000 from the General Fund Reserves, and
  that a moratorium be placed on similar grants until Council could discuss amendments to the
  Reserve Fund Policy and draft a grant agreement policy. The motion carried at a vote of 3 to
  2.

  Mr. MAZA emphasized that he would vote on this as a one-time action due to the emergency.
  Mr. MONTES requested clarification from Mr. Maloney and Ms. Andrade-Stadler and asked if
  the motion was intended for staff to create the grant agreement and move forward or if they
  would like staff to draft the agreement for Council approval at the next meeting. Mr. MALONEY
  clarified that between the original motion and the amended motion, the parameters were well
  described and that staff was equipped to follow through.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a one-time grant of $60,000 to Urban Visionaries
  for food distribution and immigrant resources for high need families in Alhambra; provided
  direction to staff regarding the grant agreement; directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize Council’s action; and placed a moratorium on any similar donations until
  such a time as a policy could be created to govern use of public funds for grants.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, ANDRADE-STADLER
  Noes:  WANG, LEE
  Absent:  NONE

RECESS & RECONVENE:  Mayor LEE called for a brief recess at 8:34 p.m. and the meeting
resumed with all Councilmembers present at 8:50 p.m.

LEE:  Vice Mayor Lee recused herself from the discussion of Item No. 1 due to property
which may be affected by the Ordinance. Ms. LEE left Council Chambers at 8:51 p.m.

PUBLIC HEARING

1.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT AN ORDINANCE APPROVING ZONING TEXT
  AMENDMENT AMD-25-03, AMENDING TITLE 23 (ZONING) OF THE ALHAMBRA
  MUNICIPAL CODE TO INCORPORATE CHAPTER 23.23 (HISTORIC PRESERVATION)
  AND OTHER ASSOCIATED AMENDMENTS, AND AMENDING CHAPTER 2.41 (HISTORIC
  PRESERVATION COMMISSION); AND DETERMINE THIS ACTION IS EXEMPT FROM
  CEQA – F2M20-51, N2M25-101, O2M25-4848, M2M25-130

  Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report and Kari FOWLER, from the
  Historic Resources Group (HRG), and Evanne St. Charles, from Architectural Resources
  Group, delivered a presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. Christine Lazzaretto,
  from Historic Resources Group, was also present to answer questions. Mr. HO stated that
  5
8-25-25
   Senior Planner McCURLEY and several Planning Commissioners were also present in the
  audience.

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M25-101 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing to consider an application for Zoning Text Amendment AMD-25-03 to adopt a Historic
  Preservation Ordinance. Zoning Text Amendment AMD-25-03 is a City-initiated application to
  adopt a Historic Preservation Ordinance establishing regulations and standards for
  designating historic resources within the City and regulating designated resources as part of
  a comprehensive Historic Preservation Program, as well as amending various sections of the
  Alhambra Municipal Code to establish consistency with the proposed Historic Preservation
  Ordinance. Adoption and implementation of a Historic Preservation Ordinance aligns with the
  goals, policies, and objectives set forth in the City’s General Plan and the City Council 2025
  Strategic Plan. The revised Historic Preservation Ordinance established regulations and
  standards for the treatment of historic resources City-wide that were intended to: 1.) Balance
  the interests of the community and individual property owners; 2.) Provide recognition of and
  protection for existing historic resources; 3.) Establish incentives to encourage rehabilitation
  and preservation of historic resources; and 4.) Add predictability to the local development
  process. The Ordinance, which would apply City-wide, established the process for determining
  a property’s status as a historic resource. Statuses included: (1) eligible or potentially eligible
  individual resource; (2) contributor or non-contributor in an eligible or potentially eligible historic
  district; (3) designated landmark; or (4) contributor or non-contributor in a designated historic
  district.

  The City’s Historic Resources Survey preliminarily identified potentially eligible individual
  resources and potentially eligible historic districts; however, further evaluation in the form of a
  Historic Resource Assessment would be necessary to determine whether a property is an
  eligible resource, and a historic resources survey report would be necessary to determine if
  an area with a grouping of resources qualifies as an eligible historic district. While the
  Ordinance did provide procedures which would allow an owner to object to a designation
  nomination, it did not allow a property owner to “opt-out” of being subject to the regulations
  and requirements implemented under the Ordinance.

  At their July 7, 2025 regular meeting, the Planning Commission conducted a public hearing to
  review the updated Historic Preservation Ordinance and adopted Planning Commission
  Resolution No. 25-04 (Attachment 2 of the Staff Report dated 8-25-25) by a vote of 7-0,
  recommending City Council approval of Zoning Text Amendment AMD-25-03, with three (3)
  additional recommendations. The Planning Commission’s recommendations were identified
  in Section 3 of Planning Commission Resolution No. 25-04 which was Attachment 2 of the
  Staff Report for this item. The proposed Historic Preservation Ordinance, along with the
  recommendations of the Historic Preservation Commission and Planning Commission, were
  presented to the City Council for final consideration and adoption. Staff also recommended
  the City Council consider an additional suggested revision, which would provide additional
  clarity in Section 23.23.090, Alterations to Historic Resources. Staff’s recommendation was to
  clarify that all contributing and non-contributing resources in potentially eligible and eligible
  Historic Districts were exempt from review; however, any designated historic landmarks,
  eligible individual historic resources, or potentially eligible individual historic resources within
  the Historic Districts would still be subject to the applicable review requirements for these types
  of individual resources.

  Finally, The City reviewed the environmental impacts of this Ordinance under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). This Ordinance was not subject to further environmental review because: (1) it
  would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there was no possibility that this
  6
8-25-25
   Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. §
  15061(b)(3)); (3) the proposed amendments would assure the maintenance, restoration,
  enhancement, or protection of the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15308); and (4) the
  Ordinance, by itself, did not constitute a “project” as defined in section 21065 of the Public
  Resources Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378). It can be seen with
  certainty that there is no possibility that this Ordinance may have a significant effect on the
  environment.

  Vice Mayor MALONEY asked for clarification regarding the different categories, including
  landmark status, eligible individual historic resources and potentially eligible resources, and
  the process to seek designation through the Historic Resources Assessment (HRA). Ms.
  FOWLER and Ms. St. CHARLES provided clarification regarding terms and process.

  Open Public Hearing:  Vice Mayor Maloney opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  The following people supported the Ordinance:
  1) Chris Olson
  2) Bert Ng, 203 S. Cordova St.
  3) Jennifer Ng, S. Cordova St.
  4) Shirley Tatsuno, 1408 S. Fifth St, also discussed her concerns with the ordinance.
  5) William Henderson, 620 N. Stoneman Ave., representing the Alhambra Chamber of Commerce
  6) Joyce Amaro, 6th St.
  7) Lewis McCammon, 105 N. Cordova St.
  8) Melissa Michelson
  9) Rosalind Sagara, representing the Los Angeles Conservancy, via Zoom
  10) Oscar Amaro, via Zoom
  11) Erica Garcia, via Zoom, representing the Planning Commission, also clarified the
  Commission’s recommendation regarding staffing.

  The following people spoke against the Ordinance:
  1) Jason Carroll, 2360 W. Main St., also distributed handouts to the Council which are on file in
  the City Clerk’s office.
  2) Andre Ransons, 809 W. Hellman Ave.
  3) Patricia Murphy, 1009 N. Granada Ave.
  4) Brett Meredith, 819 W. Commonwealth Ave., representing Atherton Baptist Homes
  5) Alborz Mohtashami, 1621 S. Monterey St.
  6) Anna Fosselman, via Zoom

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public testimony, Vice Mayor Maloney closed
  the public hearing.

  Discussion:  Councilmember WANG discussed the importance of the Historic
  Preservation Ordinance and acknowledged the concerns of the public. Ms. WANG and Mr.
  HO discussed the different categories for homes under the Historic Preservation Ordinance,
  the types of major or minor alterations allowable under the ordinance, and provisions for
  economic hardship. Mr. HO, City Attorney MONTES, and Principal Planner McCURLEY
  continued to provide clarification regarding economic hardship provisions. Ms. WANG and Ms.
  McCURLEY went on to discuss the incentives for property owners as designated landmarks,
  the eligible properties noted in the Historic Resources Assessment, and the appeal process
  for property owners. Ms. WANG supported the ordinance and requested staff explore further
  incentives for commercial and residential property owners.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked staff, Council, the consultant, and community members such
  7
8-25-25
   as the Historical Society and Alhambra Preservation Group for all their work. He supported
  the ordinance but expressed some concerns regarding commercial properties and private
  property rights. Mr. MAZA, Ms. FOWLER, and Ms. ST. CHARLES discussed the Historic
  Resouces Survey process, when residents would have to pay for a Historic Resources
  Assessment during a major alteration or demolition, identification of interior of a building during
  project review, property sales, and Accessory Dwelling Unit design oversight. Ms. McCURLEY
  also provided clarification regarding Accessory Dwelling Units. Mr. MAZA, Ms. FOWLER, and
  Ms. ST. CHARLES discussed the formation of an Historic District and the City’s ability to apply
  for State Certified Local Government Status. Mr. MAZA stated that his biggest concern was
  regarding commercial properties but stated that the ordinance could be assessed over time
  and could be improved over time.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER thanked staff, the Historic Preservation Commission,
  and the Planning Commission for their work and commented on the many changes seen in
  the community. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, Ms. FOWLER, Ms. ST. CHARLES, and Ms.
  LAZZARETTO discussed owner consent allowable under other cities’ ordinances as well as
  the provisions in the proposed ordinance. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER supported Ms. Wang’s
  suggestion for staff to explore other incentives for property owners.

  Vice Mayor MALONEY thanked staff, consultants and Commission members for their work
  and supported the ordinance. He went on to discuss governmental regulation of private
  property, acknowledged the concerns of private property owners, and the methods for property
  owners to object. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. MONTES discussed policies to address additional
  costs and the Planning Commission recommendation. Mr. MALONEY stated that he felt the
  importance of the ordinance was to protect elements which were identified in the survey, stated
  that he looked forward to further discussions of smaller details such as demolition certificates,
  briefly discussed the difficulties of downzoning, and briefly discussed the difficulties of interior
  assessment. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. MONTES discussed the supermajority vote of Council.
  He stated that he would like further discussion regarding cost to property owners, the
  application process, and technical assistance for applicants.

  Mr. MAZA motioned to approve the ordinance, which was seconded by Mr. MALONEY. Mr.
  MONTES asked for confirmation regarding changes to the ordinance including the Historic
  Preservation Commission recommendations regarding definitions of word changes to historic
  resources and properties; the Planning Commission recommendation regarding findings; and
  staff’s textual recommendation which identifies the scope of review necessary for properties.
  Mr. MAZA confirmed that these changes were included in his motion to approve. Mr. MONTES
  asked for confirmation regarding Planning Commission’s recommendations regarding financial
  assistance policies which would be drafted at a later date. Mr. MAZA confirmed that the motion
  included this direction to staff. Ms. WANG suggested that staff also look into options and
  mitigations for time and cost burdens on the property owners. Mr. MAZA agreed to the
  suggestion and added that staff review the policies of other cities. Mr. MONTES asked for
  clarification regarding the Planning Commission recommendation on the composition of the
  Historic Preservation Commission. Mr. MALONEY, Mr. MONTES, and Ms. McCURLEY
  discussed the recommendation to add a qualified historic consultant by modifying Title 2 in
  the Alhambra Municipal Code. Mr. MALONEY agreed that while there should be a qualified
  historic consultant for the commission, that the Municipal Code should not be amended to
  specifically require it.

  Action Taken:  City Council:

  1.  Conducted a Public Hearing to receive public testimony;

  2.  Directed staff to include Historic Preservation Commission recommendations
  regarding certain definitions, Planning Commission recommendations regarding
  8
8-25-25
   findings, and staff’s recommendations regarding the scope of review necessary for
  properties in the proposed ordinance; directed staff to further review the Planning
  Commission’s recommendation to consider financial assistance for the preparation of
  Historic Resources Assessments and present to Council at a later date; directed staff
  review the Historic Preservation’s recommendation to consider a reduction in building
  permit fees and present to Council at a later date; and introduced and gave first reading
  by title only, waiving further reading to the following ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M25-4848: AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA ADOPTING ZONING TEXT
  AMENDMENT AMD-25-03, AMENDING TITLE 23 (ZONING) OF THE
  ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE TO INCORPORATE CHAPTER
  23.23 (HISTORIC PRESERVATION) AND OTHER ASSOCIATED
  AMENDMENTS, AND AMENDING CHAPTER 2.41 (HISTORIC
  PRESERVATION COMMISSION)

  which ordinance shall return for a second reading and adoption at the next City Council
  meeting on September 8, 2025; and,

  3.  Determined this action was exempt from CEQA. (M2M25-130)

  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  LEE

LEE:  Mayor Lee returned to Council Chambers at 11:47 p.m.

3.  SENATE BILL (SB) 79 (WIENER), THE ABUNDANT & AFFORDABLE HOMES NEAR
  TRANSIT ACT – F2M25-19

  Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report and presentation, which is on
  file in the City Clerk’s office. SB 79 (Wiener), also known as the "Abundant & Affordable Homes
  Near Transit Act", is a California bill aimed at increasing housing density near public
  transportation stops. It would allow multi-family residential development, potentially up to
  seven stories, near train stations and bus rapid transit stops which are stops that have
  dedicated bus lanes with 15 minute or less headways during peak commuting hours, overriding
  many local zoning laws. The bill is designed to address the state's housing crisis by boosting
  housing supply, encouraging public transit use, and reducing reliance on cars. Possible
  impacts to the City of Alhambra will be focused on the southern portion of the City that may fall
  within half-mile of the CalState LA Metrolink station. The station may be considered a Tier 3
  transit-orientated development stop which could allow developments of up to 45 feet high, 60
  units per acre, and a F.A.R. of 2.0. Otherwise, there will be no direct impact to Alhambra as
  Alhambra does not have any qualifying “transit-oriented development stops” including any bus
  service meeting the standards of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 21060.2 of the
  Public Resources Code. Key aspects of SB 79 include allowing higher density housing near
  major transit stops, including apartments and other multi-family dwellings. This potentially
  includes areas currently zoned for single-family homes. The bill would also allow transit
  agencies more flexibility in developing land they own, potentially leading to more housing and
  increased ridership. It would also create statewide standards for housing developments near
  high frequency transit stops. The bill does require any proposed development would need to
  provide housing for lower income households with different percentage rates of the total units
  by different income levels pursuant to Section 50106 of the Health and Safety Code. SB 79
  has passed the California State Senate and is now in the Assembly. If passed by the Assembly
  9
8-25-25
   and signed by the Governor, it will become law and go into effect on July 1, 2026.
  Approximately, 150 cities have submitted letters of opposition through CalCities under a
  coalition.

  3) Melissa Michelson, representing the Emery Park Community Group
